title: Developer Fundamentals
summary: Why Salesforce has limits, how its apps are built, and how to pick and model the right data: clicks first, code when needed.

lessons.title: Multitenancy: Why Limits Exist
lessons.objective: Understand multi-tenant concepts and design frameworks, such as MVC architecture and Lightning Component Framework.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Salesforce runs thousands of companies on the same servers. This is called **multitenancy**. Each company gets its own **org**: private data and private setup. But they all share the same computers. If one org's code ran wild, everyone else would slow down. So Salesforce caps what one piece of work may use.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: An apartment building. Every family has its own locked flat, but they all share the water and the power. So the building has rules: nobody may run every tap at once. Where it stops: in Salesforce, breaking a rule isn't a warning. Your code stops on the spot.

cards.title: Governor limits
cards.body: Those caps are **governor limits**. They count per **transaction** (one complete run of work, from start to finish). Go over one and Salesforce throws a `System.LimitException`. You **can't catch it** with try/catch. The transaction stops and all its changes roll back.

cards.title: Numbers to know (sync / async)
items: Rows returned by SOQL: **50,000**
**DML** statements: **150**
Rows saved by DML: **10,000**
**SOSL** queries: **20**
Callouts: **100**

cards.title: Check how much you've used
cards.body: The `Limits` class tells you how much of each limit this transaction has used so far.

cards.title: Metadata-driven
cards.body: Your objects, fields and code are stored as **metadata** (data that describes your setup). The shared platform stores and serves each org's metadata. That's how Salesforce runs so many different orgs and upgrades them all automatically.

A try/catch does **not** rescue you from a governor limit. A `LimitException` can't be caught. The fix is fewer queries and fewer DML statements. Also, limits count per transaction, not per user and not per day.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **100 questions, 150 saves.** Up to 100 SOQL queries and 150 DML statements per transaction. Shared building, shared rules.

terms.say: Many companies living in one big shared computer home. Each has its own locked room for its data, but they share the same building.
Your company's own private space in Salesforce. Your data, your setup, your code. Other companies can't see inside it.
Hard rules on how much work one run of code may do. Like a referee who stops the game the moment you break a rule.
One whole job, start to finish, like saving a batch of records. Either all of it is kept or, if it fails, none of it is.
The error Salesforce throws when code goes over a governor limit. It can't be caught, so the whole job stops.
The way code asks the database a question, like "give me every Account in Paris." Each question is one query.
The commands that change data: insert, update, delete and undelete. Each command counts as one DML statement.
A text search across many objects at once, like a search box. A transaction can run 20 of them.
How long the server's brain spends working on your code. Too long, and Salesforce stops it.
Data about your setup, not your records. It describes your objects, fields and code, like the plan of a house instead of the furniture.

lessons.title: MVC: Data, Screen, Logic
lessons.objective: Understand multi-tenant concepts and design frameworks, such as MVC architecture and Lightning Component Framework.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **MVC** splits an app into three jobs. The **Model** is the data. The **View** is what the user sees. The **Controller** is the logic in between: it reacts to clicks, then reads or saves data. Keeping the jobs apart means you can change one without breaking the others.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A restaurant. The pantry is the Model: the food. The dining room and the plates are the View. The waiter is the Controller: takes your order, goes to the kitchen, brings food back. Where it stops: on Salesforce, one Apex class can serve many pages at once.

cards.title: On Salesforce
items: Model: objects, fields and relationships, like Account or `Invoice__c`
View: **Visualforce** pages, LWC HTML templates, Aura markup
Controller: standard controllers, Apex controllers and extensions, plus the JavaScript in LWC and Aura

cards.title: One page, three jobs
cards.body: The markup is the View. The Account record is the Model. The standard controller plus `AccountExt` is the Controller.

cards.title: Three kinds of controller
cards.body: A **standard controller** gives a page the same save and edit logic as a normal record page. A **custom controller** is an Apex class that holds all of the page's logic, so you rebuild save yourself. A **controller extension** adds to another controller, so you keep its actions and add your own.

cards.title: LWC fits too
cards.body: In a Lightning web component, the `.html` template is the View. The `.js` file is the client-side Controller. An Apex class with `@AuraEnabled` methods is the server-side Controller. The records it reads and saves are the Model.

Business rules that must hold everywhere don't belong in a page controller. A rule there only runs from that page. Put it with the Model, as a validation rule, flow or trigger, so it also runs for the API, imports and other screens. A **formula field** is part of the Model too.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **M**odel = **M**emory (the data). **V**iew = **V**isible (the screen). **C**ontroller = **C**ommands (the logic).

terms.say: Model, View, Controller. A way to split an app into three jobs: keep the data, show the screen, and run the logic in between.
The data part of an app. On Salesforce, that's your objects, fields and records.
The part people look at and click. The screen, the page, the buttons.
The go-between. It hears a click, fetches or saves data, and tells the screen what to show.
Salesforce's older way to build custom pages, with tags like apex:page. It still works, but new work usually uses LWC.
A ready-made controller from Salesforce. It already knows how to show, edit and save one kind of record.
An Apex class you write to run a whole page yourself. You get full control, but you must build save and the rest yourself.
An Apex class that adds extra powers to another controller. You keep the built-in buttons and add your own.
A label on an Apex method that says "Lightning components may call me." Without it, the component can't reach the method.
A field that works out its own value from other fields, like a calculator cell. Nobody types into it.

lessons.title: Lightning Components: LWC and Aura
lessons.objective: Understand multi-tenant concepts and design frameworks, such as MVC architecture and Lightning Component Framework.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: The **Lightning Component Framework** lets you build reusable pieces of screen, called **components**. There are two models. **Lightning Web Components** (**LWC**) is the modern one, built on web standards. **Aura** is the original one. To admins and users, both look like Lightning components.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: LEGO bricks. Each component is a brick you snap into pages, apps and flows. LWC bricks are the standard size every browser already knows. Aura bricks are an older, custom size. Where it stops: an Aura brick can hold LWC bricks, but an LWC brick can't hold Aura ones.

cards.title: Why LWC
cards.body: LWC uses standard **JavaScript**, HTML and **Web Components**, which browsers run natively. Less framework code has to load, so pages are fast and light. Most of what you learn carries over to any web job. Salesforce's advice: when you can choose, **choose LWC**.

cards.title: Files in an LWC bundle
items: `myCard.html`: the **template**, what shows on screen
`myCard.js`: the logic
`myCard.js-meta.xml`: settings, like where it may be used
`myCard.css`: optional styles

cards.title: Working together
cards.body: LWC and Aura can sit on the same page and talk to each other. An **Aura component can contain an LWC**. An **LWC can't contain an Aura component**. So a team can move from Aura to LWC one piece at a time.

cards.title: Where it can go
cards.body: The `js-meta.xml` file lists **targets**: the places admins may drop the component, like record pages, app pages, flows or **Experience Cloud** sites.

"Put the Aura component inside the new LWC" is the classic wrong answer. Containment only goes one way: Aura holds LWC. Another trap: Aura isn't switched off. It's still supported, so old Aura pages keep working.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Aura hugs LWC, never the reverse.** The big old Aura can carry the little new LWC, but not the other way round.

terms.say: Salesforce's kit for building screen pieces you can reuse. It covers both LWC and Aura.
Small, reusable pieces of a screen, like a card, a list or a button panel. You build one, then use it in many places.
Lightning Web Components. The modern way to build Salesforce screen pieces, using normal web code that browsers already understand.
The older Salesforce way to build components. It still works, and it can hold LWC pieces inside it.
The main language of web pages. It makes a page react when you click, type or scroll.
A built-in web standard for making your own HTML tags. Browsers understand it without extra libraries, which keeps LWC fast.
The HTML file of a component. It describes what appears on the screen.
A small settings file in every LWC. It says whether admins can see the component, and where they may place it.
The list of places a component is allowed to go, like a record page, an app page or a flow screen.
Salesforce's tool for building websites and portals for customers or partners. Components can be used there too.

lessons.title: Clicks or Code?
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, identify common use cases and best practices for declarative versus programmatic customizations, including governor limits, formula fields, and roll-up summaries.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Salesforce gives you two toolboxes. **Declarative** tools are point-and-click: fields, formulas, validation rules and flows. **Programmatic** tools are code: Apex, LWC and Visualforce. The best practice is **clicks before code**. Clicks are quicker to build, easier for admins to change, and need no test classes.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Cooking. Use a good ready-made sauce when it tastes right: fast and safe. Cook from scratch only when the recipe needs something no jar has. Where it stops: some jobs, like heavy data work or custom web services, truly need code.

cards.title: Pick the tool by the job
items: Show a value from the same record or a parent: **formula field**
Total or count child records on a master: **roll-up summary**
Block bad data with a message: **validation rule**
Update or create records when something saves: record-triggered **flow**
Complex logic, huge data sets, custom APIs: **Apex**

cards.title: When code wins
cards.body: Choose **Apex** when a flow would get too complex to follow. Choose it when you need fine control over errors and transactions, or must process millions of records in batches. And choose it for things clicks can't do, like a custom REST web service.

cards.title: Limits apply to clicks too
cards.body: Flows run inside the same **transaction** as triggers, and they share its limits. A flow's Get Records counts toward the **100 SOQL** queries. Its record changes count as **DML**. So a Get Records inside a loop can hit a limit, just like bad Apex.

cards.title: Before-save or after-save
cards.body: To change fields on the **same record** that's being saved, use a **before-save** record-triggered flow. It edits the record before it's written, so no extra DML is needed. To create or change **other** records, use an after-save flow.

"Write a trigger" is often the wrong answer. If a formula field, roll-up summary, validation rule or flow meets the need, the exam wants the click tool. Pick code only when the scenario needs something clicks can't do.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Formula shows, roll-up counts, validation blocks, flow acts, Apex does the rest.**

terms.say: Building by pointing and clicking in Setup, with no code. Like filling in a form instead of writing a program.
Building by writing code, like Apex or LWC. More power, but more work to build, test and maintain.
Salesforce's own programming language. It runs on Salesforce's servers and can read and change your data.
A field that calculates its own value from other fields. Nobody types into it.
A field on a parent that counts or totals its child records, like the total of all lines on an invoice.
A check that runs when a record saves. If the data breaks the rule, the save stops and the user sees your message.
A point-and-click automation. It can update records, create records, send emails and more, without code.
One whole job, start to finish. Everything in it shares the same governor limits and either all saves or all rolls back.
A flow that runs before the record is written. It can only change the record being saved, but it's very fast.
The commands that change data: insert, update, delete. Each one counts toward a limit.

lessons.title: Formula Fields
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, identify common use cases and best practices for declarative versus programmatic customizations, including governor limits, formula fields, and roll-up summaries.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **formula field** shows a value that Salesforce works out for you, like a spreadsheet cell. You write the formula once. Salesforce calculates the value each time the record is viewed or queried. Users can't type into it: it's **read-only**.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: The total on a shop till screen. It always shows the price of whatever is in the basket right now. Nothing is written down. Where it stops: since the value isn't saved, a formula changing never fires a trigger or a flow.

cards.title: Reaching other records
cards.body: A **cross-object formula** reaches **up** to parent records through lookup or master-detail fields, like `Account.Owner.FirstName`. It can go up to **10 relationships** away. It can't reach **down** to child records. To total children, use a roll-up summary.

cards.title: Size limits
items: Up to **3,900 characters** in the formula
Up to **1,300** characters shown after it runs
**Compile size** up to **15,000 bytes**, counting everything the formula uses
Can't use **long text area**, encrypted or Description fields

cards.title: A tiny formula
cards.body: Return types are Text, Number, Currency, Percent, Date, Date/Time, Time and Checkbox. There's no Picklist type.

cards.title: Formulas in Apex
cards.body: In Apex, you can't set a formula field: the code won't compile. After you change other fields and save, the record in memory keeps the **old** formula value. Query the record again to see the new one.

A cross-object formula shows the parent's field even to users who **can't see the parent record**. And compile size counts every formula your formula references, so a short formula can still be too big.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Formulas look up, roll-ups look down.**

terms.say: A field that calculates its own value, like a calculator that's always on. You never type into it.
You can look, but you can't change it. Like a museum painting behind glass.
A formula that borrows a field from a parent record, like showing the company's city on a contact.
The "one" side of a link. One Account is the parent of many Contacts.
A loose link from one record to another, like writing a friend's name on your card.
A tight link where the child belongs to the parent. Delete the parent and the children go too.
A field on a parent that counts or adds up its children. Formulas can't do that; roll-ups can.
How big a formula becomes once Salesforce swaps in everything it points to. It must stay under 15,000 bytes.
A field for very long text, like notes. Formulas aren't allowed to use it.
Salesforce's programming language. Code can read a formula field but can't write to it.

lessons.title: Roll-Up Summary Fields
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, identify common use cases and best practices for declarative versus programmatic customizations, including governor limits, formula fields, and roll-up summaries.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **roll-up summary** field sits on a parent record and sums up its children. It can **COUNT** the children, or find the **SUM**, **MIN** or **MAX** of a child field. Salesforce keeps it up to date whenever children change. No code needed.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A class register. The teacher's sheet (the parent) shows how many pupils came and the top test score. Each pupil (a child) feeds it. Where it stops: it only works when children are tied to the parent by **master-detail**, apart from a few standard pairs.

cards.title: Where you can create one
items: Any custom object on the master side of a master-detail
A standard object that's the master of a custom detail object
Opportunity, from its opportunity products
Account, from its opportunities
Campaign, from its campaign members

cards.title: What it can total
cards.body: **SUM** works on number, currency and percent fields. **MIN** and **MAX** also work on date and date/time fields. **COUNT** just counts children. Add **filter criteria** to include only some children, like paid invoice lines.

cards.title: Part of the save
cards.body: When a child saves, the parent's roll-up is recalculated near the end of the save. Then the **parent goes through its own save**. Its triggers, flows and validation rules run too. So a rule on the parent can block a child from saving.

cards.title: Only a lookup?
cards.body: Between two custom objects joined by a **lookup**, you can't build a roll-up summary. Keep the total with a **record-triggered flow** or an **Apex trigger** on the child. Handle insert, update, delete and undelete, or the total drifts.
A roll-up can't aggregate a formula that uses `NOW()` or `TODAY()`, or a cross-object formula. And while a roll-up exists, you **can't convert** its master-detail into a lookup.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Parent counts the kids, if they're family.** Family means master-detail. Four moves: Count, Sum, Min, Max.

terms.say: A field on a parent that counts or adds up its child records. Salesforce updates it for you.
Counts how many child records there are, like counting the pupils in a class.
Adds up a number from every child, like the total price of all lines on an invoice.
Finds the smallest value among the children, like the earliest date or the lowest price.
Finds the biggest value among the children, like the latest date or the highest score.
A tight parent-child link. The child can't live without the parent, and the parent can total the children.
Conditions that pick which children count. For example, only lines where Status is Paid.
A loose link between records. Each record lives on its own, so roll-up summaries don't work between custom objects.
A no-code automation that runs when a record is created, changed or deleted.
Code that runs by itself when records are saved or deleted. It can keep totals up to date.

lessons.title: Objects, Fields and Relationships
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, determine, create, and access the appropriate data model including objects, fields, relationships, and external IDs.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Your **data model** is the set of objects, fields and links that hold your data. An **object** is like a table, a **field** is a column, and a **record** is a row. Standard objects come with Salesforce, like Account. **Custom objects** are ones you build; their names end in `__c`.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A school database. Students and Classes are objects. A student's name is a field. "This student is in this class" is a **relationship**. Where it stops: Salesforce relationships also decide deleting and sharing, not just linking.

cards.title: Relationship types
items: **Lookup**: a loose link. The child keeps its own owner and sharing.
**Master-detail**: a tight link. The detail inherits owner and sharing. Delete the master, the details go too.
Many-to-many: a **junction object** with two master-detail fields
Hierarchical: a special lookup on User, like Manager

cards.title: Master-detail rules
cards.body: Each custom object can have up to **2 master-detail** relationships and **40 relationships** in total. The master-detail field is **required** on the detail. Details can't move to another master unless you tick **Allow reparenting**. A standard object can't be the detail of a custom object.

cards.title: Owner and sharing
cards.body: A detail record has no owner of its own: its owner is the master's owner. So a custom detail object **can't have sharing rules, manual sharing or queues**. If the child needs its own owner, use a lookup.

cards.title: Many-to-many
cards.body: To link many students to many classes, build a junction object, like `Enrollment__c`, with a master-detail to each. The **first** master-detail you create is the primary one. It sets the record owner and the look. Deleting either master deletes the junction records.

You can't add a master-detail field to a custom object that **already has records**. Create a lookup, fill it on every record, then convert it. And linking an object to itself needs a **lookup**, not master-detail.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Master-detail = family**: the kids share the parent's life. **Lookup = friends**: linked, but each lives on its own.

terms.say: The plan of how your data is stored: which objects exist, what fields they have, and how they link.
A kind of thing you store, like Accounts or Invoices. Think of it as a table.
One piece of information on a record, like Name or Phone. Think of it as a column.
One single item, like one customer or one invoice. Think of it as a row in the table.
Tables you add yourself. Their API names end in __c, like Invoice__c.
A link between two objects, so a record can point to another one, like a contact pointing to its company.
A loose link. The child points at a parent, but keeps its own owner and its own sharing.
A tight family link. The detail has no owner of its own and goes away when the master is deleted. You can only move it to a new master if Allow reparenting is on.
A middle object that joins two others, so many of one can link to many of the other. Like an enrollment list joining students and classes.
Rules that open up record access to more people. A detail can't have its own, because it follows its master.

lessons.title: External IDs and Related Data
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, determine, create, and access the appropriate data model including objects, fields, relationships, and external IDs.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Other systems have their own numbers for records, like an order number from your warehouse system. An **External ID** field stores that number on the Salesforce record. Then code and data loads can find, update and link records by the outside number, without first looking up the Salesforce **record Id**.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A library card with your student number written on it. The library knows its own card number, the school knows the student number, and either one finds you. Where it stops: if two cards carry the same number, matching breaks, so make the field Unique.

cards.title: Upsert
cards.body: **Upsert** means insert or update in one step. It matches on the record Id, an External ID field, or a standard field with `idLookup`. No match: insert. One match: update. **Two or more matches: error**, and that record isn't saved.

cards.title: Upsert by External ID
cards.code:
List<Order__c> orders = buildFromErp();
upsert orders Erp_Number__c;
cards.body: Matches each order on `Erp_Number__c`. New numbers create records; known numbers update them.

cards.title: Setting it up
cards.body: Mark a custom text, number, email or auto-number field as External ID. Each object can have up to **25**. External ID fields are **indexed**, so lookups on them are fast. Tick **Unique** as well, so duplicate numbers can't sneak in.

cards.title: Link to a parent with no query
cards.body: The stand-in Account holds only the External ID. Salesforce finds the real **parent** and links it.

cards.title: Query related data
cards.code:
SELECT Name, Account.Name,
  (SELECT Subject FROM Cases)
FROM Contact
cards.body: Go **up** to a parent with dots, like `Account.Name`, up to 5 levels. Go **down** to children with a **subquery** on the child relationship name, like `Cases`.

To walk a custom relationship in SOQL, use `__r`, not `__c`: `Invoice__r.Total__c`. The field that holds the Id is `Invoice__c`. A subquery uses the **relationship name**, like `Line_Items__r`, not the object name.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Dots go up, subqueries go down.** `__c` holds the Id, `__r` opens the door.

terms.say: A field that stores another system's number for a record. Like writing your student number on your library card so both places can find you.
Salesforce's own unique code for every record, like 001… for an Account. Every record gets one.
Update it if it exists, insert it if it doesn't. One command, two possible results.
A setting on some standard fields that lets upsert use them to find a match, like an External ID.
A setting that stops two records from having the same value in a field.
Kept in a sorted list, like a book's index, so Salesforce finds matching records fast.
The "one" side of a link, like the Account that many Contacts belong to.
A small query inside a bigger one. It brings back each parent's children in the same result.
The name SOQL uses to walk a link. For custom links it ends in __r, like Invoice__r.
The ending for a custom relationship in SOQL. It means "open the linked record," while __c is the field holding its Id.

lessons.title: Agentforce for Developers
lessons.objective: Understand use cases and limitations of using Agentforce for Developers.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Agentforce for Developers** is an AI helper for writing Salesforce code. It runs in **VS Code** as part of the Salesforce Extension Pack. It suggests code as you type, answers questions in a chat, explains code, and drafts Apex, LWC and **test classes**. Its newest version is called **Agentforce Vibes**.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A co-pilot on a driving lesson. It reads the road and suggests moves fast. But you hold the wheel, and the drive is your responsibility. Where it stops: a co-pilot rarely bluffs, but an AI can be confidently wrong.

cards.title: Good uses
items: **Inline autocomplete**: finish a line of Apex, JavaScript or HTML as you type
Chat: turn a plain-English request into code
Explain or document code you didn't write
Draft test classes as a starting point

cards.title: Limitations
cards.body: AI output is **nondeterministic**: the same prompt can give different code. It can compile and still have logic bugs. It can miss **bulkification**, governor limits or security checks. It doesn't replace **code review**, real tests or your judgment.

cards.title: Trust and data
cards.body: You choose what goes into a prompt, so you're responsible for it. Never paste passwords, API tokens or real customer data. Share only the code and context the AI needs. Check your company's rules for AI tools before you start.

cards.title: Review AI code like this
items: Are SOQL and DML **outside** loops?
Does it handle 200 records, not just one?
Does it respect sharing, CRUD and **FLS**?
Do tests assert real results, not just "not null"?

cards.body: "The AI wrote it, so it's ready for production" is the classic wrong answer. Generated tests can reach 75% coverage and still check nothing. A developer must review and test the code before deploying it.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **AI drafts, you decide.** A fast first draft, then a slow, careful review.

terms.say: An AI helper for Salesforce developers. You describe what you want, and it suggests or writes code for you to check.
Visual Studio Code, a free code editor. Salesforce developers add Salesforce tools to it as extensions.
Apex code that checks your other code works. Salesforce needs tests before code can go to production.
The newest name for Salesforce's AI coding tool. The exam still calls it Agentforce for Developers.
Grey suggested code that appears as you type. Press Tab to accept it, or keep typing to ignore it.
You can't predict the exact answer. Ask the same thing twice and you may get two different results.
Writing code that handles many records at once, like 200, instead of one at a time. It keeps code under governor limits.
A careful read of code by a person, looking for bugs and risks before it ships.
Field-level security. Rules about which fields each user may see or edit, like hiding Salary from most people.

flashcards.front: Why does Salesforce have governor limits?
flashcards.back: Many orgs share the same servers (multitenancy). Limits stop one org's code from using up shared resources and slowing everyone else.

flashcards.front: Can you catch a governor limit error with try/catch?
flashcards.back: No. A `System.LimitException` can't be caught. The transaction stops and all its changes roll back.

flashcards.front: How many SOQL queries and DML statements can a synchronous transaction run?
flashcards.back: 100 SOQL queries (200 async) and 150 DML statements. Up to 50,000 rows from SOQL and 10,000 rows saved by DML.

flashcards.front: Do governor limits reset between chunks of a Batch Apex job?
flashcards.back: Yes. Each `execute` call gets a fresh set of limits.

flashcards.front: What are the three parts of MVC on Salesforce?
flashcards.back: Model: objects, fields and relationships. View: Visualforce markup, LWC and Aura templates. Controller: standard controllers, Apex controllers and extensions, and component JavaScript.

flashcards.front: When do you use a controller extension instead of a custom controller?
flashcards.back: When you want to keep a controller's built-in actions, like the standard Save, and add your own logic on top.

flashcards.front: What must a custom controller provide that a standard controller gives for free?
flashcards.back: All the page's actions, including save. A custom controller doesn't inherit any standard behaviour.

flashcards.front: Which is recommended for new components: LWC or Aura?
flashcards.back: LWC. It's built on web standards, runs natively in browsers and performs better. Aura is still supported.

flashcards.front: Can an LWC contain an Aura component?
flashcards.back: No. An Aura component can contain an LWC, but an LWC can't contain an Aura component.

flashcards.front: Which LWC file says where a component can be placed?
flashcards.back: The `js-meta.xml` configuration file, through `isExposed` and its targets, like `lightning__RecordPage`.

flashcards.front: What's the general rule when clicks and code can both do the job?
flashcards.back: Clicks before code. Declarative tools are faster to build, easier to change and need no test classes.

flashcards.front: Do flows count toward governor limits?
flashcards.back: Yes. Flows share the transaction's per-transaction limits with Apex. Each Get Records counts as a SOQL query.

flashcards.front: When should you use a before-save record-triggered flow?
flashcards.back: To update fields on the same record that's being saved. It's fast and uses no extra DML. Use after-save to change other records.

flashcards.front: Name two jobs that usually need Apex instead of clicks.
flashcards.back: A custom REST or SOAP web service, and heavy processing of very large data sets, such as Batch Apex.

flashcards.front: How far can a cross-object formula reach?
flashcards.back: Up to parent records, as far as 10 relationships away. It can't reach down to child records.

flashcards.front: What are the main formula field size limits?
flashcards.back: 3,900 characters in the formula and 1,300 characters displayed. Compile size, which counts every field and formula it references, can be at most 15,000 bytes.

flashcards.front: Does a formula field changing value fire a trigger?
flashcards.back: No. The value is calculated when read, so no record is saved and no trigger or flow runs.

flashcards.front: Can Apex set a formula field?
flashcards.back: No. Formula fields are read-only, so assigning one is a compile error.

flashcards.front: Which relationship does a roll-up summary need?
flashcards.back: Master-detail, for custom child objects. A few standard pairs also work, like Account from Opportunity.

flashcards.front: What can a roll-up summary calculate?
flashcards.back: COUNT of children, or the SUM, MIN or MAX of a child field. Filter criteria can limit which children count.

flashcards.front: What happens to the parent when a roll-up is recalculated?
flashcards.back: The parent goes through its own save, so its triggers, flows and validation rules run. A parent rule can block the child's save.

flashcards.front: How do you total children over a lookup between custom objects?
flashcards.back: With a record-triggered flow or an Apex trigger on the child. Handle insert, update, delete and undelete.

flashcards.front: How many relationships can a custom object have?
flashcards.back: Up to 2 master-detail and 40 relationships in total.

flashcards.front: Why can't a custom detail object have sharing rules?
flashcards.back: Detail records have no owner of their own. Their owner is the master's owner, so sharing rules, manual sharing and queues aren't available.

flashcards.front: How do you model many-to-many?
flashcards.back: A junction object with two master-detail fields, one to each object. The first master-detail is the primary one and sets the owner.

flashcards.front: Can you add master-detail to an object that already has records?
flashcards.back: Not directly. Create a lookup, fill it on every record, then convert it to master-detail.

flashcards.front: What does upsert do when it finds 0, 1 or 2+ matches?
flashcards.back: 0 matches: insert. 1 match: update. 2 or more matches: error, and that record isn't saved.

flashcards.front: Which field types can be External IDs, and how many per object?
flashcards.back: Custom text, number, email and auto-number fields. Up to 25 per object.

flashcards.front: How do you link a child to a parent without querying the parent's Id?
flashcards.back: Set the relationship to a stand-in parent that holds only its External ID, like `new Account(Erp_Id__c = 'A-1')`. Salesforce finds the parent.

flashcards.front: When do you use `__c` and when `__r` in SOQL?
flashcards.back: `__c` is the field holding the parent's Id. `__r` walks the relationship, like `Invoice__r.Name`, or names a child subquery.

flashcards.front: What can Agentforce for Developers do?
flashcards.back: In VS Code it suggests code as you type, turns prompts into code, explains and documents code, and drafts test classes.

flashcards.front: What are the main limitations of Agentforce for Developers?
flashcards.back: Output can differ for the same prompt and can be wrong. It may miss bulkification, limits or security. A developer must review and test it.

flashcards.front: What should you never put in a prompt?
flashcards.back: Passwords, API tokens or real customer data. Share only the code and context the AI needs.

questions.q: A new developer asks why Apex code has hard limits on queries and DML statements. What is the main reason?
options: The limits apply only to trial orgs and are lifted once licenses are bought
Apex is compiled to Java, so the limits come from the Java virtual machine
Each org runs on its own dedicated server, and the limits match that server's fixed hardware size
Many orgs share the same servers, so no single org's code may hog shared resources
questions.explain: Salesforce is multitenant: many orgs share one set of servers. Governor limits stop one org's code from slowing down everyone else.
wrong: Every org has governor limits, including production orgs with paid licenses.
The limits come from the shared, multitenant design, not from Java.
Orgs don't get their own server. They share the same infrastructure.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: What is the maximum number of SOQL queries a synchronous Apex transaction can issue?
questions.explain: A synchronous transaction can run 100 SOQL queries. Asynchronous Apex gets 200.
wrong: 50 is the limit on `@future` calls, not on queries.

200 is the limit for asynchronous Apex, not synchronous.

questions.q: A developer runs this Anonymous Apex to load 200 contacts. Each contact has an `AccountId`. What happens?

The first 100 contacts are saved, and the other 100 fail with a `DmlException`
All 200 contacts are saved, because the limit is counted separately for each record in a trigger
Salesforce combines the queries into one, so the code runs within limits
questions.explain: Governor limits count per transaction, and going over one stops it. The trigger runs one query per contact, so query 101 throws a `LimitException` and everything rolls back.
wrong: A limit error rolls back the whole transaction. Nothing is partly saved.
All the trigger's queries share one transaction and one limit of 100.
Salesforce never merges queries for you. Each one counts.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: Which two statements about Apex governor limits are true? (Choose 2)
options: An admin can raise the SOQL query limit in Setup for one org
Limits reset each time a new trigger fires in the same transaction
Most limits are counted per transaction

Limits apply only to code that runs as an integration user
questions.explain: Limits are counted per transaction. Going over one throws a `LimitException`, which no catch block can handle.
wrong: Governor limits are fixed by Salesforce. Setup can't change them.
Every trigger in one transaction shares the same limits.
Limits apply to all Apex, whoever runs it.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

wrong: No DML has run yet at the start, so the count is 0.
100 is the SOQL query limit, not the DML limit.
There is no 200 DML statement limit for asynchronous Apex either. It's 150.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: A developer runs this code synchronously to total contacts for 120 accounts. A teammate wrapped it in try/catch "so a limit error can't break the save." What happens?

The catch block logs the error and execution continues, so `insert summaries` saves the partial totals
Salesforce switches the job to async limits, so all 120 queries succeed
The loop skips the extra accounts, and `insert summaries` saves the first 100
questions.explain: A `LimitException` can't be caught. Query 101 ends the transaction at once, so the catch block and the insert never run.
wrong: The catch block never runs for a limit error.
Salesforce never switches a running transaction to async limits.
Apex doesn't skip loop steps to stay under a limit.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: A synchronous process needs about 150 SOQL queries and can't easily be refactored this release. Which two ways let it run under higher query limits? (Choose 2)

Move the work into a Queueable job
Move the work into an `@future` method
Run the code as a user with Modify All Data
Call the code from a before trigger instead
questions.explain: Asynchronous Apex gets higher limits, like 200 SOQL queries. Queueable and `@future` both run asynchronously.
wrong: Try/catch doesn't change any limit.
Permissions don't change governor limits.
A trigger runs in the same synchronous transaction, with the same limits.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: A developer creates 200 opportunities with one `insert` statement. This trigger then runs. What is the result?
options: 200 DML statements succeed, because each trigger gets its own separate limit of 200 DML statements
150 tasks are saved and the last 50 are quietly skipped
200 DML statements are attempted, and number 151 throws a `LimitException`
One DML statement, because Salesforce bulkifies an `insert` inside a loop by itself
questions.explain: Each `insert` inside the loop is a separate DML statement. The limit is 150 per transaction, so statement 151 fails and everything rolls back.
wrong: Triggers share the transaction's limit of 150 DML statements.

Salesforce never combines DML statements for you.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: A synchronous query has no `WHERE` clause and runs on an object with 80,000 records. What happens?

questions.explain: A transaction can retrieve at most 50,000 rows with SOQL. Asking for more throws a `LimitException`.
wrong: 2,000 is the row limit for one SOSL query, not for SOQL.

questions.q: In Salesforce, what does a single transaction mean for governor limits?

One request's work, start to finish, under one set of limits
One trigger run, with a fresh set of limits given to every trigger that fires
Everything one user does during one day
questions.explain: A transaction is one complete unit of work, like saving a batch of records. All code and automation in it share one set of governor limits.
wrong: One query is just a part of a transaction.
Triggers in one transaction share the same limits.
Limits don't count per user per day.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

wrong: A `LimitException` can't be caught.

A `LIMIT` caps rows, but each query in the loop still counts.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: This Batch Apex job updates 1 million leads in chunks of 200. Each `execute` call runs 3 queries and 1 DML statement. Will the job hit the 100-query limit?

wrong: Each chunk starts with fresh limits, so the count never adds up.

questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: Saving a case runs a before-save flow with two Get Records elements, and then an Apex trigger with three SOQL queries. How do these count against the SOQL limit?
options: The flow and the trigger each get their own limit of 100
Flows count against a separate limit of 2,000 elements
All 5 queries count against the same transaction's limit of 100
Only the trigger's 3 queries count, because flows are exempt from Apex limits
questions.explain: Flows run inside the same transaction as triggers and share its limits. Each Get Records counts as a SOQL query, so this save uses 5 of 100.
wrong: One transaction has one set of limits for all its automation.
Get Records counts toward the SOQL limit like any query.
Flows are governed by the same per-transaction limits as Apex.

questions.q: An architect explains why customizations survive Salesforce's three releases a year. Which statement best describes the platform design behind this?

wrong: Orgs don't get private copies of Salesforce code.

questions.q: `Shipment__c` already has two master-detail relationships. It now needs a link to `Carrier__c`. What should the developer create?

A junction object
A lookup field
A third master-detail field
questions.explain: A custom object can have at most 2 master-detail relationships. Other links must be lookups, within the total of 40.
wrong: A roll-up summarizes children. It doesn't create a link.
A junction object is for many-to-many, which isn't needed here.
A third master-detail would pass the limit of 2.

questions.q: `Invoice_Line__c` is the detail of `Invoice__c`. The relationship was created with default settings. A developer moves a line to another invoice with this code. What happens?

The change is rejected, because reparenting isn't allowed by default
The line moves only if the user owns both invoices

wrong: A master isn't deleted when it loses a detail.
It would, but only if Allow reparenting were turned on.
Ownership doesn't control reparenting.
questions.source: Salesforce Help: Object Relationships Overview

questions.q: What is the main purpose of marking a custom field as an External ID?
options: To let the field hold more than 255 characters
To hide the field from users who don't own the record
To hold another system's id so records can be matched by it
To make the field the record's Salesforce Id
questions.explain: An External ID holds the record's id from another system. Upserts and data loads can then match records by it.
wrong: It doesn't change the field's length.
External ID has nothing to do with visibility.
The Salesforce record Id is separate and can't be replaced.

questions.q: `Erp_Id__c` is an External ID on Account but isn't marked Unique. Two existing accounts both have `E-77`. A developer runs this code. What happens to the Fabrikam record?
options: It updates the newer of the two accounts
It updates both accounts
It's inserted as a third account
It fails with an error and isn't saved
questions.explain: Upsert needs one match. No match inserts, one match updates, and several matches give an error for that record.
wrong: Upsert doesn't pick a winner between matches.
Upsert never updates two records for one input.
Insert only happens when nothing matches.

questions.q: `Erp_Number__c` is a unique External ID on `Order__c`. `ORD-1` already exists in Salesforce, and `ORD-2` doesn't. What does the upsert do?
options: Inserts both, because upsert always creates new records
Fails, because the list mixes new and existing records
Updates `ORD-1` and skips `ORD-2`
Updates `ORD-1` and inserts `ORD-2`
questions.explain: Upsert matches each record on the External ID. A match is updated, and no match is inserted.
wrong: Upsert updates when it finds a match.
Mixing new and existing records is exactly what upsert is for.
Upsert inserts records that don't match.

questions.q: A developer links a new contact to its account by the account's External ID. No account has `Erp_Id__c = 'A-9999'`. What happens?

The contact is inserted with a blank account
A new account with `Erp_Id__c = 'A-9999'` is created automatically
questions.explain: A stand-in parent with an External ID must match an existing record. If no parent matches, the DML fails.
wrong: The stand-in is only a reference, so it doesn't need a Name.

The parent is only created if you insert it yourself in the same statement.

questions.q: `Invoice_Line__c` has a master-detail field `Invoice__c`, and `Invoice__c` has a lookup `Customer__c` to Account. Which query returns each line with its customer's name?

`SELECT Id, Invoice__r.Customer__r.Name FROM Invoice_Line__c`
`SELECT Id, Invoice.Customer.Name FROM Invoice_Line__c`
`SELECT Id, Invoice__c.Customer__c.Name FROM Invoice_Line__c`
questions.explain: To walk a custom relationship, swap `__c` for `__r`. Dots go up from child to parent at each step.
wrong: Every custom relationship step needs `__r`, including `Customer__r`.
Custom relationships keep their full name with `__r`.
`__c` is the Id field. You can't walk through it.

questions.q: A developer needs each account's name and the last names of its contacts in one query. Which query works?
options: `SELECT Name, Contacts.LastName FROM Account`
`SELECT Name, (SELECT LastName FROM Contacts) FROM Account`
`SELECT Name, (SELECT LastName FROM Contact) FROM Account`
`SELECT Name FROM Account JOIN Contact ON AccountId`
questions.explain: To go down to children, use a subquery on the child relationship name. For contacts on Account it's `Contacts`, the plural.
wrong: Dot notation only goes up to a parent, not down to children.
A subquery uses the relationship name, not the object name.
SOQL has no `JOIN` keyword.

questions.q: `Line_Item__c` is the detail of `Invoice__c`. The master-detail field's child relationship name is `Line_Items`. Which query returns invoices with their line amounts?

`SELECT Name, (SELECT Amount__c FROM Line_Item__c) FROM Invoice__c`
`SELECT Name, (SELECT Amount__c FROM Line_Items__r) FROM Invoice__c`
`SELECT Name, (SELECT Amount__c FROM Line_Items) FROM Invoice__c`
questions.explain: A custom child relationship in a subquery is its relationship name plus `__r`. Here that's `Line_Items__r`.
wrong: Relationship names end in `__r`, not `__c`.
A subquery uses the relationship name, not the object name.
Custom relationship names need the `__r` ending.

questions.q: Every night, an ERP sends thousands of orders, some new and some changed. The developer wants no duplicates and as few queries as possible. Which two steps should the developer take? (Choose 2)
options: Delete all orders each night and insert the full list again
Mark `Erp_Number__c` as External ID and Unique
Query each order by `Erp_Number__c` inside the loop before saving
Save the orders with `upsert orders Erp_Number__c;`
Insert all orders with `Database.insert(orders, false)`
questions.explain: Upsert by a unique External ID updates known orders and inserts new ones in one statement. Unique stops duplicate numbers.
wrong: Deleting and reloading loses history and wastes DML.
A query per order wastes queries and can hit the limit.
Plain insert creates duplicates of orders that already exist.

questions.q: `Erp_Code__c` is an External ID that's Unique and set to treat "ABC" and "abc" as different values. A `Customer__c` record with `ACME-1` already exists. What does this code do?

upsert c Erp_Code__c;
options: Both values are changed to uppercase
The upsert fails with a duplicate value error
A new record with `acme-1` is inserted
The existing `ACME-1` record is updated

wrong: Salesforce doesn't change the case of your data.
They count as different values, so there's no duplicate.
The values differ in case, and this field is case-sensitive.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Upserting Records

questions.q: How many levels up can a single child-to-parent relationship path go in a SOQL query, as in `Contact.Account.Owner.FirstName`?
